title: How do you monitor Flink jobs: Flink Web Dashboard (job graph, checkpoints, backpressure, exceptions), Flink Metrics (latency, throughput, checkpoint duration, state size) exposed to Prometheus/Grafana/Datadog, and what metrics indicate trouble (increasing checkpoint duration, growing state size, backpressure on specific operators)?
shortTitle: How do you monitor Flink jobs and what metrics indicate trouble
keyPoints: The Flink Web Dashboard shows the job graph, per-operator backpressure, checkpoint history, watermark progress, and recent exceptions.
The Flink metrics system exports time series like records-in/out per second, latency, checkpoint duration, state size, and buffer usage to Prometheus or Grafana.
Steadily increasing checkpoint duration means state is growing or the state backend is under pressure, risking checkpoint stalls.
Continuously growing state with no plateau signals a state leak, often keyed state that is never cleaned up.
Backpressure concentrated on one operator identifies the bottleneck; everything upstream slows behind it.
Rising Kafka consumer lag means the job is slower than the input rate, tying back to backpressure or insufficient parallelism.
Alert on trends and rates of change rather than only absolute values for early warning before outages.

s1_definition.oneliner: Use the Flink Web Dashboard for live inspection and export Flink metrics to Prometheus or Grafana, watching checkpoint duration, state size, backpressure, and consumer lag as the key danger signs.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Flink Web Dashboard** – A built-in UI served by the JobManager that visualizes the job graph, per-operator backpressure, checkpoint history, watermarks, and exceptions.
- **Flink Metrics System** – Exports numeric time series through reporters (Prometheus, Datadog) for dashboards, historical trends, and alerting.
- **Key throughput metrics** – numRecordsInPerSecond and numRecordsOutPerSecond per operator.
- **Key checkpoint metrics** – lastCheckpointDuration, lastCheckpointSize, and completed/failed checkpoint counts.
- **Key state metrics** – State size per operator, visible via checkpoint size.
- **Key backpressure metrics** – busyTimeMsPerSecond, backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond, idleTimeMsPerSecond per operator.
- **Consumer lag** – For Kafka sources, records-lag-max tells whether the job is keeping up with input.
s1_definition.analogy: Running a Flink job at the National Bank of India is like running the payments processing line in a branch. The Web Dashboard is the live camera feed on the wall: you see each station, whether any station has a queue forming behind it, and whether the overnight safe-backup finished on time. The metrics system is the set of sensors wired to head office (Prometheus and Grafana), recording throughput, delays, and backup times minute by minute, with alarms that page the on-call engineer when something trends the wrong way.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Monitoring a Flink job combines the built-in Web Dashboard with the metrics system exported to Prometheus and Grafana. The Web Dashboard is the first stop for live inspection: it shows the job graph, per-operator backpressure, checkpoint history, watermark progress, and recent exceptions. For continuous monitoring, the Prometheus reporter exports metrics that Grafana visualizes with dashboards and alerts.

The real skill is interpreting the metrics. Steadily increasing checkpoint duration means state is growing or the backend is under pressure. Continuously growing state with no plateau signals a state leak. Backpressure concentrated on one operator identifies the bottleneck. Rising Kafka lag means the job is slower than the input rate. The senior insight is to alert on trends and correlate metrics: backpressure plus rising lag plus a busy operator points straight at the culprit.

At the National Bank of India, our real-time fraud job started missing latency targets. Rather than guess, I read the metrics. State size was climbing with no plateau, checkpoint duration was lengthening, the fraud operator's backpressure was rising, and Kafka lag was increasing. Correlating those told a single story: the fraud operator had a state leak that made it the bottleneck. The fix was adding state TTL, after which state plateaued, checkpoints shrank, backpressure cleared, and lag drained.

Being able to name which metric reveals which failure mode, correlate them into a root cause, and alert on trends instead of reacting after a crash is exactly what keeps a production streaming platform healthy.

Remember one sentence: Monitor checkpoint duration, state size, operator backpressure, and Kafka lag, and correlate them to find the root cause before the job crashes.
